Evaluation: Analysis of performance data reveals that while communication improves prediction of health and shield dimensions (reducing variance compared to without communication), there is a persistent and significant deficiency in predicting absolute coordinates (e.g., s[2], s[7], s[12], s[17], s[22] for agent X; s[26] for enemy X). With-communication mean accuracy for agent absolute X is around 0.6–0.7, only marginally better than without communication and in some cases worse. Variance across agents for these dimensions is low, indicating a systematic failure rather than imbalance. For health/shield dimensions (e.g., s[0], s[5], s[15], s[20], s[24]), with-communication still shows moderate variance (up to 0.0022), with occasional outlier agents (e.g., agent 4 in s[20] early phase at 0.895 vs others ~0.98), indicating residual information asymmetry. The current protocol shares single-timestep features (movement possibilities, relative enemy position, health, shield, attack flag) but fails to provide sufficient temporal and behavioral context for accurate absolute position inference.
Missing_Information_Hypothesis: The primary missing information is the temporal sequence of each agent's own actions (especially movement directions) and health/shield changes over time. Without a history of movement actions, other agents cannot integrate velocities to estimate absolute positions relative to a common reference. The current static can_move flags only encode boundary constraints but not continuous displacement. Additionally, the lack of sharing own absolute position estimates (which could be derived from can_move and known map dimensions, but map size may not be known) forces agents to rely on relative observations that are inconsistent across perspectives. The single-timestep health/shield values cause residual variance because sudden changes (e.g., after enemy attack) are not propagated well to all agents.
Improvement_Suggestions: 1. Replace the static message with a temporally extended one: for each agent, broadcast a sequence of the last 10 timesteps of its own features. Include: (a) last action move directions (indices 38–41) and attack flag (42) as binary vectors per timestep, (b) own health ratio (34) and shield ratio (35) over the sequence. This provides a trajectory that other agents can use to track position and infer damage events. 2. Retain the existing 11 single-timestep features (enemy visibility, rel enemy x/y, own health, attack flag, can_move, shield, distance to enemy) but now append the temporal sequence as additional dimensions. For example, per agent, the message becomes 11 (current) + 10*(6 action+2 health/shield) = 11+80=91 dimensions. Concatenate messages from all 4 other agents (total 364 appended dims). 3. To manage dimensionality, consider compressing the temporal sequence via a small recurrent encoder (e.g., GRU) into a fixed-size embedding before sharing. 4. Add explicit sharing of each agent's survival status (e.g., whether agent is alive) to prevent wasted computation on dead agents. 5. Ensure that the temporal sequence includes the exact timesteps where prediction disagreements are highest (e.g., after enemy engagement phases), which can be identified from the phase analysis (e.g., early-mid and mid for absolute X).
